content.title: About
content.content: A doughnut is a piece of fried or baked dough, often glazed, dusted with powdered sugar, or filled with jam, cream, or other fillings. This entry refers to the cake‑type doughnut finished with a coating of powdered sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 17th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
The classic American doughnut is ring‑shaped with a hole in the middle.
In Russia, “ponchiks” without a hole are common and are often served with jam or condensed milk.
Powdered sugar not only decorates but also creates a light, crisp crust.
In Japan, “dorayaki” style doughnuts are covered with sweet glaze and sprinkles.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide a quick boost of energy thanks to their carbohydrate content, making them a convenient snack.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: The dough is rich in starch, which is easily digested and absorbed.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and yeast used in the batter contain small amounts of vitamins B1, B2 and B6.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: In modest amounts doughnuts supply iron, magnesium and phosphorus.

items.title: Powdered sugar as quick glucose
items.content: Powdered sugar can rapidly raise blood glucose, which may be helpful in cases of hypoglycemia.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Deep‑frying creates trans fats that are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The batter usually contains wheat, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Doughnuts are calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised for those monitoring their weight.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert, paired with coffee or tea, added to ice cream, or used as a base for layered cakes topped with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator, or freeze for up to 2 months.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg Omelet with Cheese and Dark‑Green Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet prepared with cream cheese and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach, broccoli or kale) is a nutritious breakfast or light dinner. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, cheese adds calcium and a creamy flavor, and the greens are rich in vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cream cheese is often used in omelets to create a smoother texture.
Dark‑green vegetables contain chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Eggs are one of the few foods that contain all essential amino acids.
An omelet can be cooked quickly on a skillet in 5–7 minutes.
Around the world omelets are served with different add‑ins: in Japan with seaweed, in Spain with potatoes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A large egg provides about 6 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese contributes calcium for bone health and a small amount of vitamin D.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and cheese are good sources of vitamins B2, B12 and biotin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from green vegetables
items.content: Spinach, broccoli and kale supply vitamins C, K, folate and lutein, helping protect cells.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs or milk proteins may experience reactions, up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Cream cheese can be salty, so choose low‑sodium versions if you watch salt intake.

items.title: Foodborne illness from undercooking
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; cook until the whites are fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk, stir in grated cream cheese, chopped dark‑green vegetables, salt and pepper. Cook in a lightly oiled skillet, stirring gently until the mixture sets but remains tender. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a little oil to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey eggs are the eggs of the domestic turkey, larger than chicken eggs, with a speckled, cream-colored shell. They have a rich yolk and a flavor similar to chicken eggs, though slightly richer. Turkey eggs are less commonly sold than chicken eggs and can be cooked in the same ways.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A turkey egg is noticeably larger than a chicken egg.
The shell is cream-colored with small brown speckles and is thicker than a chicken eggshell.
Turkey hens lay far fewer eggs per year than chicken hens, which is why the eggs are rarely sold.
The flavor is similar to a chicken egg, with a slightly richer taste.
Turkey eggs can be used in the same ways as chicken eggs.

items.title: Source of high-quality protein
items.content: Turkey eggs provide complete protein with all essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Eggs are a source of choline, a nutrient involved in normal cell function.

items.title: Provides vitamins
items.content: Turkey eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2), vitamin A, and small amounts of vitamin D.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Turkey eggs contain selenium, phosphorus, and iron.

items.title: May help you feel full
items.content: Protein-rich foods may increase the feeling of fullness.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to chicken eggs may also react to turkey eggs.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Raw or undercooked eggs may carry Salmonella and should be avoided by pregnant women, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain dietary cholesterol. People with certain health conditions should ask a healthcare professional how many eggs are suitable for them.

items.title: Availability and freshness
items.content: Turkey eggs are less standardized than chicken eggs, so buy from a reliable source and avoid cracked or dirty eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey eggs can be boiled, fried, scrambled, poached, or baked, and used in omelets and baking. One turkey egg is roughly equal to about two chicken eggs. Cook until the white is set and the yolk is firm, and allow slightly longer for boiling because of their size.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store turkey eggs in the refrigerator in their carton, away from strong-smelling foods. Use them within about three to five weeks of purchase or by the date given by the seller. Hard-boiled eggs should be refrigerated and eaten within about a week. Do not use cracked or dirty eggs.
